articles.title: Over 100 areas under state of calamity due to El Niño
articles.summary: A total of 106 cities and municipalities across the country have been officially declared under a state of calamity as the effects of the ongoing El Niño phenomenon continue to intensify, the…

blocks.text: Pedestrians brave the heat along United Nations Avenue as the midday sun beats down on March 5, 2026.
STAR / Ryan Baldemor

MANILA, Philippines — A total of 106 cities and municipalities across the country have been officially declared under a state of calamity as the effects of the ongoing El Niño phenomenon continue to intensify, the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Council (NDRRMC) said.
In its latest report on Tuesday, October 6, the NDRRMC said the dry spell has affected 104,149 families, or 388,375 people.
The following are the numbers of areas under a state of calamity per region:

items: Region 2: 66 cities/municipalities
CARAGA: 23 cities/municipalities
Region 5: 12 cities/municipalities
CALABARZON: Four cities/municipalities
Region 12: One city/municipality

blocks.text: Out of the 35,893 families identified as requiring urgent assistance, the government has successfully assisted 24,618 families.
The total cost of assistance provided so far stands at P39,058,681.06, distributed as follows:

items: CARAGA: P23,091,638 provided to 11,672 families
Region 2: P9,927,750 provided to 1,891 families
Region 5: P6,039,293.06 provided to 11,055 families

blocks.text: The agricultural sector has also suffered losses.
Citing data from the Department of Agriculture, a total of P5,580,172,296.84 in damages was recorded.
The dry conditions have affected 201,660 farmers and fisherfolk, damaging 223,830.19 hectares of crop areas and resulting in a production volume loss of 117,037.69 metric tons.
Region 2 recorded the highest agricultural damage, accounting for over P4.96 billion of the total losses.

In the CARAGA region, 39 wild, forest, and mountain fire incidents have been reported. CARAGA has also experienced water supply interruptions across four cities and municipalities, though supplies have since been restored.
Due to the extreme conditions, 33 cities and municipalities in CARAGA were forced to suspend classes.

articles.title: NBI confirms Velasco couple owns 2 alleged ‘cash houses’ in Pasig
articles.summary: The NBI said Velasco spouses own 2 alleged “cash houses” in Pasig and are linked to 2 Marinduque resorts under investigation.

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Initial validations by the National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) have confirmed that former House Speaker Lord Allan Velasco and his wife, Rowena, own two alleged "cash houses" in Pasig City, along with two beach resorts in Marinduque that are being probed for suspicious financial activities.

NBI Director Melvin Matibag said on Tuesday, October 6, that they have established the ownership following the claims of dismissed policeman Rodulfo Gracioso Jr. that Velasco and his wife bought properties to store large volumes of cash during the lawmaker’s term as House speaker.

“Basically, nitong mga nakaraang araw ang vinalidate natin ‘yung claim niya doon sa cash houses na sinasabi and we’re able to establish, dun sa seven cash houses na sinasabi, we’ve already established two that are owned by Velasco spouses,” Matibag said.

(Basically, these past few days, we validated his claims about cash houses, and we’re able to establish that among the alleged seven cash houses, we’ve already established two that are owned by Velasco spouses.)
Both houses were located in Valle Verde 2 in Pasig: one on Champaca Street, and another on Sampaguita Street, according to Matibag.
The NBI said investigators checked land titles and Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) records in validating the ownership.
'Cash houses'
In his affidavit, Gracioso claimed Velasco was the primary source and coordinator of multi-million-peso cash deliveries to Vice President Sara Duterte.
The cash, he claimed, came from the 25% “all-in” kickbacks on government projects across the country.

He said the cash was initially packed and stored at the residence of Velasco and his wife at No. 142 Sampaguita St., Valle Verde 2, but the money grew too large, which made the former lawmaker buy at least six additional houses where they could store the money.
Velasco and Duterte have earlier denied Gracioso’s claims.
The NBI said the established ownership of the two houses in Pasig by Velasco has so far supported Gracioso’s claims.

“Dun sa mga claims ni Mr. Gracioso ng bahay at pag-aari ng mga Velasco, tumatama na. Especially lalo na doon sa bahay because ‘yung bahay it was named under Eagle Assets and Realty na ang presidente nito si Ms. Rowena Velasco,” Matibag said.

(The claims of Mr. Gracioso on residences and properties are beginning to be validated. Especially on the houses, because the houses were named under Eagle Assets and Realty, whose president is Ms. Rowena Velasco.)
Resorts in Marinduque
Aside from the houses in Pasig, the NBI said it also looked into Gracioso’s claims that Velasco was investing a lot of money into two resorts at Poctoy White Beach in Torrijos, Marinduque.
Matibag said the Sara Resort and Cabanas and Amara Resort and Villas were both linked to the Velasco spouses.
“Napakalaking resort niyan. When we checked sa SEC ‘yung ownership, lumalabas na sa spouses Velasco. May mga inassign na na-share without consideration. So ini-investigate natin ‘yan,” Matibag said.
(That is a very big resort. When we checked the ownership on the SEC, it appears to belong to spouses Velasco. There were shares assigned without consideration. So we’re investigating that.)

NBI said the Sara Resort and Cabanas is operated by 888 Wealth Star Corp, where Rowena Velasco serves as president and chairman, holding 60% of the shares. The P20 million capital, the agency said, was reported to be fully paid in cash at incorporation.

The Amara Resorts and Villas, meanwhile, is operated by Amara Equity Ventures Inc., where Velasco and his wife were principal incorporators holding 80% of subscribed shares. The NBI said both transferred their original shareholdings to third parties in 2023, but Rowena remained a stockholder while serving as vice president.

The NBI said they are investigating the link between the two resorts as SEC records showed that the same individuals are serving as officers in both, while the incorporators share the same address. Individuals handling corporate filings for one resort also appeared on the records of the other.
Matibag said they will continue to investigate crucial documents to identify how these properties were acquired, who the owners are, and where the funds came from.

articles.title: Germany's ex-spy chief arrested for espionage
articles.summary: August Hanning served as the head of Germany's BND foreign intelligence agency from 1998 to 2005. According to German media, he is being investigated for allegedly passing on state secrets and…

image.caption: August Hanning has reportedly been arrested over alleged spying and acting as a secret service agentImage: Michael Kappeler/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Police have arrested the former head of Germany's BND foreign intelligence agency, August Hanning, on suspicion of espionage, the federal prosecutor's office announced Tuesday.
Hanning served as the agency's chief between 1998 and 2005.

According to a statement from the prosecutor's office, he is facing charges including alleged espionage against the state, disclosure of state secrets, attempted treason, and working as a secret service agent.

The statement added that a former high-ranking employee of the BND had also been arrested on suspicion of providing Hanning with hundreds of classified documents in exchange for money over more than a decade.
What else do we know about the investigation?
Police arrested Hanning early Tuesday at his home in Nordwalde near the western German city of Münster, according to information from WDR, NDR and the Süddeutsche Zeitung.
Hanning's alleged accomplice, who was identified only as Manfred D. in line with Germany's privacy laws, was taken into custody in Bavaria.
Authorities were conducting searches at both suspects' properties, as well as in Berlin, the prosecutor said.
During Hanning's tenure as spy chief, D. reportedly served as his chief of staff. He is facing charges of aiding and abetting attempted treason and espionage against the state.

articles.title: Giant underwater Kelvin wave could 'pack a punch' for B.C. in mid-October
articles.summary: A giant underwater wave of water connected to this year's El Niño weather pattern is making its way up the west coast of the Americas, raising alarm bells amongst scientists worried about how climate…

image.caption: Waves and debris crash into the breakwater in Victoria, B.C. in 2024. This year's El Niño will soon send more waves at B.C.'s coast. (Chad Hipolito/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Science

A giant underwater wave of water connected to this year's El Niño weather pattern is making its way up the west coast of the Americas, raising alarm bells amongst scientists worried about how climate change is magnifying the impacts of the naturally-occurring phenomenon.
El Niño phenomenon could worsen the effects of storm surges and high tides
· CBC News
· Posted: Oct 06, 2026 4:00 AM EDT | Last Updated: 31 minutes ago

A giant underwater wave of water connected to this year's El Niño weather pattern is moving up the west coast of the Americas, raising alarm bells among scientists about how climate change is magnifying the impacts of the naturally occurring phenomenon.
The so-called Kelvin wave is not unexpected. But like El Niño as a whole, it is happening on top of human-caused climate change that has already warmed the oceans and atmosphere.

A smaller wave already reached B.C. earlier this summer, and the next one is expected to arrive within one to two weeks, according to Bill Merryfield, a research scientist at Environment and Climate Change Canada.
"We actually did already see over 30 centimetres in some locations in June. And so the coming wave looks like it'll be a stronger one," Merryfield said.
What causes it?

The Kelvin wave is a naturally occurring weather phenomenon, just like El Niño itself. In normal years, winds blow from east to west along the equator in the Pacific Ocean, generally pushing water from South America toward Asia.
During El Niño years, however, those east-to-west winds weaken or can reverse direction, allowing water to move east instead.

"When these Kelvin waves reach the coast of South America, there's nowhere further east for this pile up of water to go. And so it splits and starts running up and down the coasts of the Americas" and eventually all the way up to Canada, Merryfield said.
Sea-level monitoring data collected at Tofino, on Vancouver Island's Pacific coast, shows the impact of the earlier Kelvin wave in June.
Rather than a giant tsunami-like wave, the Kelvin wave temporarily raises sea levels.

"You can think of it more like a very broad, hundreds of miles wide, but very shallow bulge in the height of the ocean surface, so by maybe a foot or so," University of California climate scientist Daniel Swain told CBS News last month.
What will it do to the West Coast?
Merryfield said the impacts are most pronounced during king tides, particularly high tides that happen when the gravitational pull of the sun and moon combine to produce higher-than-normal tides.

"So if you put that 30 centimetres of sea level rise on top of a king tide, and then maybe you add a winter storm to that, which causes a storm surge, that's when you really start to get into trouble," he said.
"This extra foot or so of sea level rise due to El Niño can pack a punch."
El Niño-fuelled heat could kill half a million people by February: study

Those surges could be intensified by another effect of El Niño, further raising sea levels along the B.C coast. El Niño can strengthen northward winds along the coast, pushing even more water toward shore.

These compounding effects — the Kelvin wave, stronger northward winds and winter storms, on top of climate change already raising sea levels and intensifying extreme weather — could worsen flooding and erosion along the coast. Strong El Niños in the past have caused widespread erosion on California's beaches.
Local authorities there are placing emergency sand on beaches and expect the Kelvin wave to raise water levels six to 12 inches, the Associated Press reports.
The impacts of the Kelvin wave — and El Niño more broadly — could extend far beyond this season, Merryfield warned.

The oceans absorb much of the excess heat trapped by greenhouse gases, moderating global warming as humans continue to burn fossil fuels. During El Niños, however, some of that stored heat is released from the ocean into the atmosphere.
This will likely lead to 2027 becoming the warmest year on record "by quite a significant margin," Merryfield said, echoing similar warnings from other climate research organizations and scientists.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Inayat Singh covers the environment and climate change at CBC News. He is based in Toronto and has previously reported from Winnipeg. Email: inayat.singh@cbc.ca

articles.title: 'Only the beginning': Anti-immigration group says Ottawans should 'brace themselves'
articles.summary: For weeks, posters and stickers across Ottawa advertising the anti-immigration group Dominion Society of Canada — which is calling for mass deportations of millions of people — have been generating…

image.caption: A screenshot from a video posted by the Dominion Society of Canada shows members gathering in Hamilton, Ont. The ethno-nationalist group wants an end to and reversal of Canada's immigration and multicultural policies dating back decades, and to punish the people and organizations that created, ran a

blocks.text: For weeks, posters and stickers across Ottawa advertising the anti-immigration group Dominion Society of Canada — which is calling for mass deportations of millions of people — have been generating complaints of racism and white nationalism online, to police and to the city.
But Ottawa police say the posters and stickers reported so far do not constitute hate crimes, and the group's chair and founder Daniel Tyrie said the recruitment campaign is not going to stop.
"Posters and stickers are only the beginning. Ottawa residents should brace themselves," Tyrie told CBC News in an email last week.
"Those demanding that we stop recruiting should get used to disappointment. We are organizing, we are growing, and we are not going away."

The Dominion Society is a registered non-profit corporation based in Ottawa, established in 2025. It had rented a virtual office at the Château Laurier hotel near Parliament Hill from the company Regus until September, when it moved under unclear circumstances to another virtual office at 222 Queen St.

The group has been organizing postering campaigns across the country since its founding last year. It generated headlines this summer in southern Ontario where it tried to organize and hold a convention in Hamilton but ended up relocating to Burlington after community protests and statements against them.
The group believes only anglophone and French people with English, French, Irish and Scottish settler ancestry qualify as Canadian, "later joined by further waves of Europeans."

It's unclear if the society considers all Indigenous people Canadian. The society's website states that First Nations are among Canada's founding groups alongside European settlers, but says First Nations have since become either Anglo-Canadian or French Canadian through "ethnogenesis" with the settlers over generations — "a new people ... born of European roots."

items: Hamilton mayor asks businesses to be aware of anti-immigration group planning conference in area
Far-right Austrian white nationalist, permanently banned from U.K., plans to attend Hamilton conference
Hamilton police join call for venues to 'consider the impact' of hosting anti-immigration group Saturday
Protesters rally at Hamilton City Hall against anti-immigration group
'We didn’t want them:' Hamilton rallies against Dominion Society, as group holds event in Burlington, Ont.

blocks.text: The group wants to end and reverse Canada's immigration and multicultural policies dating back decades, and to punish the people and organizations that created, ran and enabled them, according to its website.

The Dominion Society wants all temporary foreign workers deported, birthright citizenship and naturalized citizenship restricted and revoked, permanent resident status revoked, dual citizenships eliminated, and any immigrants who have not sufficiently assimilated to be deported.
What would their version of Canada look like?

In the Dominion Society's version of Canada, no kosher (Jewish) or halal (Islamic) meat production would be allowed, business and government signage in any languages other than English and French would be banned, and "public institutions — including schools, media, and the civil service — will be required to promote assimilation, unity, and shared national values, not group-based identity politics," its website states.

The Canadian Multiculturalism Act would be struck down and replaced with the National Cohesion Act, which would "affirm Canada's founding as a historically European, Christian, and bicultural (English and French) nation with a common civic identity," the site continues.
The society has no clear answers about how many years of immigration it wants to reverse, or what an acceptable level of assimilation would be.

In an interview with CBC by phone, Tyrie said he believes things took a turn for the worse in the 1960s and again under Justin Trudeau's government starting in 2015, and that turning back the immigration clock to that year would be "a very fair and reasonable cut-off, unfortunately, even for people that have integrated into our society, with the exception of people who have married Canadians."
'An environment that is less welcoming'
Tyrie believes "mass immigration and radical demographic changes" are today's "most pressing" issues.
He insists his group's deportation policies aren't based on ethnicity.

"The English, the Anglo-Canadians, the franco-Canadians and the First Nations need to work together to collaboratively protect our unique identities, which can't be found anywhere else in the world," Tyrie said by phone.

He thinks the state has made Canada uncomfortable for "actual Canadians," and that "putting in place programs to prioritize people from other countries, people from foreign cultures, ahead of our own, I think that's hateful."

"We can build an environment that is less welcoming, more hostile to foreign cultures, foreign languages, foreign people in order to make them also want to leave and go back to their home country where they can continue to build, be within a community that is consistent with their values, their culture, their religion," Tyrie said.
'We can do much better than this in Ottawa'

Ottawa resident Sarah Fraser first saw the Dominion Society's posters Sept. 24 on Bank Street at Billings Bridge, and others in a nearby residential area. They appeared racist to her, with the word "remigration" and pictures featuring white people exclusively in wartime, so she took them down.
"I was furious, actually, that these posters were in my neighbourhood and that there was an effort to recruit into this group in my neighbourhood," Fraser said in an interview last week.

"We can do much better than this in Ottawa. We need to build communities of care. We need to reach out to our neighbours and our friends and our families to be more open about racism and hate ... to take action within our own spheres of influence to make sure that these ideas do not spread," she said.
"The ideas are so far beyond inappropriate, they're unwelcome in my Ottawa."
Fraser understands that for people who are struggling, the idea that one change could solve all the country's problems "would be fantastic."

"But the world is quite complex, and anything that sounds too good to be true, probably is," Fraser said. "I would hate for folks to go from, 'I'm feeling uncomfortable,' to, 'I think other people should be hurt in order for me to feel more comfortable.' That's not a good place for folks to start. Let's not put our own comfort over someone else's safety."
What is the Dominion Society of Canada?
'Encourage the powers that be to take some action'
Evan Balgord is executive director of the non-profit organization Canadian Anti-Hate Network, and has researched the rise of the far-right movement in Canada for years.

He calls the group the "suits and ties" political arm of the white nationalist movement in Canada, "seeding the ground for a political idea to take root. And the political idea they want to take root is racist mass deportations."

"When you dig into what they actually say in their podcasts in their own audience, they are talking about removing citizenship from people who are Canadians and deporting them on the basis of race, religion and ethnicity. They are advocating for ethnic cleansing when they call for remigration.... That's my opinion, but it's pretty clear," Balgord said.
Two of the "hallmarks of hate" in Canadian law include targeted groups of people being blamed for society's problems, and that removing targeted groups of people is the solution, Balgord noted.
"I believe that the Dominion Society of Canada's entire message hinges around exactly those points and is in violation of the law," he said.

People offended by the Dominion Society's views and goals should continue to take their posters and stickers down, Balgord said, but they should also be asking their elected officials what law enforcement and the government are doing about the group's leaders.

"Take [the materials] down, cover them up, call your MP and ask them ... 'Why aren't the leaders of this organization calling for racist mass deportations being charged? Why are they allowed to have a non-profit corporation [in Canada]?'" Balgord said.

"Encourage the powers that be to take some action here, because it's been 10 years of white nationalist growth in Canada. These guys have gotten emboldened enough now that they're out there harassing communities, and we don't want it to happen anymore."
Posters don't meet criminal threshold, police say

The Ottawa Police Service first became aware of the Dominion Society of Canada's posters and stickers in December 2025. As of last week, police had received 18 reports from the public about the materials in Alta Vista, Barrhaven, Kanata South and Rideau-Vanier, the force wrote in an email to CBC.
None of the reported content constitutes a possible hate crime, police said.

"Each report is assessed individually and in context to determine whether it meets the legal threshold for a criminal offence. To date, the posters, on their face, have not met that threshold," police wrote.
"We recognize the community’s concerns and appreciate those who have come forward."
Ottawa's bylaw department had received four complaints about the posters and stickers as of last week.
Staff removed the materials in each case, according to Jake Gravelle, the city's chief of bylaw and regulatory services.

The city "is committed to fostering a safe, respectful and inclusive community for all residents," and people "who encounter signs, posters or other materials that may contravene municipal regulations are encouraged to submit a report to the City through 3-1-1."
Suspected crimes should be reported to police, Gravelle added.

articles.title: The small African nation ready for Messi's big night
articles.summary: Benin are about to have their own moment in the limelight as they visit Argentina for Lionel Messi's final game.

blocks.text: One of Benin's best-known players is their captain, Steve Mounie.
The forward plays for German Bundesliga side FC Augsburg, but will also be known to Huddersfield Town fans having played for the club between 2017-2020.
He's been a regular with the national side for more than a decade but says he's never played a game for them outside of Africa.
"When the coach called me and told me about this game. We didn't know it was going to be the last game of Leo Messi," Mounie told BBC Sport.
"It was like the cherry on top of the cake. It adds some more values to this big event for Benin, and it's going to be a big event for the world of football."
However, injury means Mounie will play no part in the game. Instead of staying at home recovering, however, he says this was not a moment he could miss out on.
"I cannot play," he said. "I just came to join the team, to support the team. And, I need to be honest with this because football is my passion. I came for myself.
"I even paid for my own ticket to come here.
"I would prefer to be on the bench, but if they tell me that I need to be in the stand, I will be in the stand. There is no problem, but I want to see the game from a pitch view."

The former Premier League striker says, while the result of the friendly is largely inconsequential, those players who are selected will know it's a great chance to enhance their reputations and that of Beninese football.

"We are a team that is very disciplined," said Mounie. "We have a lot of young talent in the team right now that have good technical skills. We are always willing to go forward. We play pressing football, but when we cannot, we stick together and we fight.
"We are a team like a family, And I think we can relate to this Argentina team because they feel like they are like a family too, which Messi is a father to."
Argentina warmed up for the fixture against Benin by defeating fellow west African side Burkina Faso 7-0.
Many will be predicting a similar scoreline this game - and it's unlikely Messi will play the full 90 minutes.

A more likely scenario is that, with Argentina a few goals to the good, Messi will be substituted in the second half, allowing the sold-out crowd at Estadio Monumental to say farewell to their country's greatest sports star.
Once the final whistle does go - don't be surprised if there's a rush towards the World Cup-winning captain.
"To get hold of a Messi match-worn shirt is incredibly tough because everybody knows how valuable they are," said Doug Bierton, founder of Classic Football Shirts.
"So every player on the pitch is looking to swap with him. It's the first time a legend has bowed out with a special edition shirt."
Bierton, whose private collection of iconic football shirts reaches into the thousands, says the last match-worn Messi shirt would be collector's dream.
He ranks it in the same category as Diego Maradona's shirt worn when he scored his 'Hand of God' goal against England at the 1986 World Cup. A jersey which sold for £7.1m in an auction in May 2022.

Another item considered in that realm is Zinedine Zidane's shirt from the last time he played for France - which ended in a red card after being sent off for headbutting Italy's Marco Materazzi in the 2006 World Cup final.
The fact Messi's shirt is being worn in a friendly - yet considered in such high regard - is perhaps testament to the belief he is the greatest footballer ever.
So Bierton predicts it won't be just Benin players who will be after the jersey.
"I'm sure some of his team-mates will be too, he's good friends with [Rodrigo] De Paul," he said. "He'll probably be after it as well. Does he get a gift, a retirement present?
"The kit man will be after it. Who knows? I'm literally going to watch the match just to see who he swaps shirts with."

articles.title: Children brave snipers and mortars to go to school near Yemen front line
articles.summary: In rare access to Taiz, the BBC World Service speaks to children, teachers and families affected by the war.

blocks.text: Image source, Liam Weir / BBC
Rafeef says the journey to school terrifies her, but she is determined to keep going
ByNawal Al-Maghafi
Reporting fromTaiz, Yemen
Every morning at 6am, 10-year-old Rafeef and her younger brother get ready for school, putting on their cream and brown uniforms.
She always looks forward to seeing her friends and learning about everything from maths to Arabic and Islamic studies. She can't wait to start studying English next year.
But for Rafeef, the journey to school involves far greater risks than crossing roads or missing the bus.

Her school in Taiz, south-western Yemen, stands on a mountain at the edge of a valley known as no-man's land - a heavily contested front line in the civil war between forces supporting Yemen's internationally recognised government, which is backed by Saudi Arabia, and the Iran-backed Houthis.
On one side of the school is government-held territory, on the other are Houthi sniper positions.
Rafeef's home is further down the mountain.
Every time she goes to school, she has to walk uphill with her back towards the snipers. "I'm afraid," she says.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Rafeef's school is overlooked by Houthi positions on the mountains beyond the valley

blocks.text: Rafeef's school is overlooked by Houthi positions on the mountains beyond the valley
According to Unicef, roughly 3.2 million children in Yemen were out of school even before the war escalated last month.
It says thousands of children have been killed or maimed since the war began in 2014, while thousands more have been recruited by armed groups on both sides.
Yet despite the risks, Rafeef says she does not want to stop going because she loves seeing her friends and it is her only chance to be with them. She begins naming the children in her classroom.
Going to school is the only time Rafeef's parents let her go outside. They say they are keen for her to get an education and have the chance of a better life. Rafeef hopes to become a doctor.
'A mortar came out of nowhere'
Rafeef's family moved to Taiz from the coastal city of Hudaydah nine years ago, seeking safety when Houthis took control there.
But Taiz has also endured fighting.
Rafeef says that two years ago there was a mortar attack outside her new home.
"Everyone was out except for me and my brother. Then a mortar came out of nowhere… shrapnel blew through the door and into the house." Her arm was broken and there is still a scar where she was hit.

And in recent days the conflict has intensified. On Sunday the Houthis cut off a vital supply route linking Taiz to Aden, which meant they were able to effectively encircle Taiz. Control of that route has kept shifting.
Residents have told the BBC they are afraid the Houthis could seize the city at any moment.

Government forces have made gains in other areas this week, they say, retaking control of strategic points on the Bab al-Mandab Strait - a key shipping chokepoint - and launching an offensive to try to regain control of the capital, Sanaa.
Homes in Taiz are mostly scattered across the slopes, but many have been abandoned by families fleeing the fighting.
Twice, we try to visit the neighbourhood where Rafeef and her family live, but a community leader advises us it is too dangerous.
On the first occasion, residents of the neighbourhood tell us that three people have been shot by snipers. On the second, we are told of another shooting.
At Rafeef's school, one of the teachers, Abdel Raqeeb al-Obaidi, 45, takes us on to the rooftop to show us what he says are Houthi military camps, barracks and sniper positions in the mountains.
Standing on the rooftop, a Yemeni security adviser accompanying us suddenly tells us to go back inside. We are visible from these positions and could be shot, he says.
Abdel Raqeeb laughs, acknowledging the danger. He says the school has been fired on before.
"The situation may explode at any moment while we are sitting in class or sleeping or we are in school or we are out on the street. We do not know how our future is and how tomorrow is."
For Abdel Raqeeb, the risk has become routine. His familiarity with it is unsettling.

blocks.caption: A map of Yemen, showing the position of Sanaa in the west, Taiz in the south-west, and Aden on the south-west coast. The Bab al-Mandab Strait to the south-west tip of Yemen is also marked. The Red Sea is to the west of the country, and Saudi Arabia is to the north of Yemen.

blocks.text: Taiz has long been a major battleground in the country's devastating civil war. After ousting the government from the capital Sanaa in 2015, the Houthis attempted to also seize control of Taiz but were driven out of most of the city by local militiamen.
Seizing Taiz would give the Houthis full control over the country's north. Now, in their latest offensive, Houthis are making extensive use of drones alongside other weapons.
Sometimes civilians are collateral damage in the fighting.
Later that evening, we get a call from a hospital about a five minute drive away from the school. Two children have been badly injured by a mortar strike.
When we arrive at Al-Rawdah Hospital, we see a nurse standing outside the intensive care unit, holding a tiny pair of beige, rubber sandals that are splattered with blood.
They belonged to Ahmed, a three-year-old boy who we learn was killed when a mortar struck a mechanic's shop in the city.

blocks.caption: Image caption, The shoes a three-year-old boy, Ahmed, was wearing when he was hit by a mortar

blocks.text: The shoes a three-year-old boy, Ahmed, was wearing when he was hit by a mortar
Shrapnel in the heart
When I ask about the shoes, the nurse, Ikram Shamsan, begins to cry.
"What did this child or his family ever do wrong?" she asks.

Ahmed was killed when a piece of shrapnel pierced his heart, entering through his back. The boy had been with his father, who was getting his motorcycle tyre pumped up at the mechanic's shop. The father was unharmed.
A doctor tells us the father had intended to leave his son at home, but the boy cried because he wanted to come too.
As he takes his son's body from the hospital, the father asks how he will face the boy's mother.
Completing a simple errand turned into the worst day of their lives.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Amjad's mother does not know if he will survive after he was injured by shrapnel

blocks.text: Amjad's mother does not know if he will survive after he was injured by shrapnel
Another boy, 11-year-old Amjad, was also at the mechanic's shop. He and his brother worked there with their uncle, sending money to their family in their home village.
Shrapnel has struck Amjad in his lung and abdomen. When we reach him, he is in intensive care, struggling to breathe. No relatives are beside his bed.
His doctor describes his condition as critical and fears he could die within hours. He hopes his mother will arrive in time to say goodbye.
Amjad was admitted at about 20:00 that evening. His mother reaches him at around 06:00 the following morning, delayed by the eight-hour journey from the village.
She sits beside his bed and prays, trying to remain composed. Once outside the room, she falls to her knees and breaks down.
Doctors say his heart rate improves during her visit. They judge him stable enough for another operation.
He has since undergone that surgery, but remains critically ill.
"We're always terrified. It's devastating to see children killed," says nurse Shamsan. "We want peace and we want to be safe."
Additional reporting by Jasmin Dyer

articles.title: Sara Duterte denies Gracioso cash delivery allegations
articles.summary: Vice President Sara Duterte rejected allegations by dismissed policeman Rodulfo Mondigo Gracioso Jr. that he delivered suitcases of cash to her and members of her family.

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Vice President Sara Duterte rejected allegations by dismissed policeman Rodulfo Mondigo Gracioso Jr. that he delivered suitcases of cash to her and members of her family.
Duterte said Gracioso’s sworn statement and media interviews falsely linked her to events that she neither committed nor had knowledge of or personally experienced.

“Mariin kong tinatanggi ang mga pahayag ni Rodulfo Mondigo Gracioso Jr. sa kaniyang sinumpaang salaysay at mga panayam sa media na iniuugnay ako sa mga pangyayaring hindi ko ginawa, hindi ko nalalaman, o hindi ko personal na naranasan,” Duterte said during a livestreamed press briefing on Tuesday, October 6.

(I strongly deny the statements made by Rodulfo Mondigo Gracioso Jr. in his sworn affidavit and media interviews linking me to events that I did not commit, was not aware of, or did not personally experience.)
The vice president said her camp would submit her affidavit to authorities on Thursday, October 8.

Gracioso has alleged that he delivered cash to Duterte, Davao City 1st District Rep. Paolo “Pulong” Duterte and former President Rodrigo Duterte upon the instructions of former House Speaker Lord Allan Velasco.
Duterte disputes Gracioso’s claims
Duterte rejected Gracioso’s account that he fetched her from a private hangar in Pasay, drove her in a white Ford Savanna van and brought her to Diamond Hotel.
She said the Presidential Security Group handled her security from July 2016 to June 2022 and that her flights during that period were arranged through the PSG.
"Hindi kailanman nangyari na ako ay sinundo ni Gracioso sa isang private hangar sa Pasay, sumakay sa isang Ford Savanna White na artista van at hinatid sa Diamond Hotel," she said.
(It never happened that Gracioso picked me up at a private hangar in Pasay, where I boarded a white Ford Savana artist van and was taken to Diamond Hotel.)
She also said she did not own such a vehicle and that there were no records showing she visited Diamond Hotel.
Duterte questioned why she would need to speak with or thank Gracioso, saying she could communicate directly with Lord and his wife Rowena “Wen” Velasco.
She also denied that Royce Chocolate was her favorite, saying she seldom eats sweets because she is diabetic.
Duterte rejected Gracioso’s claim that former Davao City chief information officer Jefry Tupas was her personal aide who received cash on her behalf.
“Hindi ko katiwala, assistant, or personal staff si Tupas,” she said.
(Tupas is not my trustee, assistant, or personal staff.)

Duterte said she believed Gracioso included Tupas in his allegations because he mistook their friendship and Tupas’ attendance at her events as a sign that he was her subordinate. She also accused Gracioso of targeting Tupas because of homophobia.
She likewise denied owning a Hermes bag or a Patek Philippe watch.
Photos as rebuttal
Duterte presented photos of her activities to dispute Gracioso’s claims about her whereabouts in April 2019.
She said she was in Davao City for her mother’s birthday on April 14, followed by campaign rallies in Mati and Tagum on April 15, Digos on April 16, and Koronadal and Tacurong on April 17.
She said she spent April 18 to 20 at Island Buenavista before attending an Easter Egg Hunt in Davao City on April 21.
Her itinerary also showed trips to Cotabato City and Kidapawan on April 22, Malaybalay and Valencia on April 23, Puerto Princesa on April 24, and Bongao, Tawi-Tawi and Jolo, Sulu on April 25.
Duterte also disputed Gracioso’s claim that he went to her house, saying the property was too small to have the receiving area he described.
“Ang ibig sabihin lamang nito ay hindi nakapunta si Gracioso sa bahay namin dahil hindi niya alam kung anong itsura ng bahay namin,” she said.
(This simply means that Gracioso never went to our house because he did not know what our house looked like.)
She denied receiving vehicles or having an aide named “Kuya Tony.”
Duterte also denied knowing Ramil Madriaga, who identified himself as her former aide and bagman.
“Kung kunyaring totoo ang maleta na may P20 million na binigay kay Ramil Madriaga, sa bahay ko pa mismo, nakakapagtaka na hindi ito binanggit ni Madriaga,” she said.
(If the suitcase containing P20 million that was supposedly given to Ramil Madriaga at my house were indeed true, it is surprising that Madriaga did not mention it.)
She also rejected Gracioso’s claim that cash from Velasco was used to buy a motorcycle, saying she bought it in December 2017.
Velasco connection
Duterte said she believes Gracioso was among the men tasked by Rowena Velasco to monitor her husband.
“Paliwanag ni Lord, ang grupo ng mga lalaki ay ‘padala’ ni Wen na mga tagabantay upang mag-report sa kanya kung si Lord ay nambababae,” Duterte said.
“Ayon sa mga larawan ay naniniwala ako na si Gracioso ay isa sa mga taong tinutukoy ni Lord noon na tagabantay sa kanyang pangbababae,” she added.

Duterte said she met the Velascos during her father’s presidency, when Rowena introduced herself as a businesswoman close to San Miguel Corp. president Ramon Ang. She said Rowena also introduced her husband, who was then a politician in Marinduque.
NBI probes Gracioso's claims
Meanwhile, the National Bureau of Investigation continues to look into Gracioso’s allegations.
NBI Director Melvin Matibag said investigators are validating the claims through records and other means and are not relying on Gracioso’s lie detector test.

The NBI has found that two properties identified by Gracioso as “cash houses” are owned by the Velascos. Investigators are also checking corporate, tax and financial records involving properties and businesses linked to the couple.
Matibag said these records showed that some of Gracioso’s claims about the Velascos’ relationship and assets were consistent with available documents, although the investigation remains ongoing.
The Velascos, through their lawyers, have previously denied Gracioso’s allegations.

articles.title: Keeping up with the Bolsonaros: Flávio’s surprise first-round election win heralds rise of a political dynasty
articles.summary: Four members of disgraced ex-president Jair Bolsonaro’s family have been elected to office, most notably his wife and son Flávio, who won the first round of voting to be Brazil’s new…
articles.byline: Tiago Rogero in Rio de Janeiro

blocks.text: The weekend’s elections in Brazil not only put Jair Bolsonaro’s eldest son, Flávio Bolsonaro, in the lead in the presidential race, but also underscored how far the former president has come in building a political dynasty.

As his far-right senator son heads into a runoff against the leftist incumbent, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, a sweeping far-right victory in congressional races also secured seats for Jair Bolsonaro’s wife, two of his sons and one of his brothers.
Few in the family have spent much time working outside politics since the patriarch led the way four decades ago, but the offices they now hold have had a significant upgrade.

Former first lady Michelle Bolsonaro, 44, who divided her campaign with caring for her husband as he serves a sentence under house arrest for attempting a coup, ran for public office for the first time and was elected senator.

blocks.caption: Former first lady and senate candidate for the Liberal Party (PL), Michelle Bolsonaro, campaigning in Brasília.   Photograph: Sérgio Lima/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Bolsonaro’s second son, Carlos Bolsonaro, 43, regarded as the most radical of the siblings – he ran his father’s social media accounts and was indicted by federal police for leading a so-called hate cabinet that spread fake news and attacks on opponents – was also elected senator for the first time.

His previous political career amounted to 25 years as a city councillor in Rio de Janeiro – starting at the age of 17, when his father put him up for a seat against his own mother, Rogéria Bolsonaro, who had divorced Jair. Carlos won. (Rogéria also ran last Sunday for a seat in the state legislature, still using the Bolsonaro surname, but lost.)

blocks.caption: From left, Jair, Michelle and Carlos Bolsonaro riding in an open car after Jair Bolsonaro’s swearing-in ceremony in 2019.   Photograph: André Penner/AP

blocks.text: The patriarch’s fourth son, Jair Renan Valle Bolsonaro, 28, who dropped his two middle names on the ballot to run simply as Jair Bolsonaro, jumped from city councillor to federal congressman.
Of Bolsonaro’s five children, only his 15-year-old daughter has never held political office.

Even the former president’s younger brother, Renato Bolsonaro, 62, nicknamed the “brother who can’t win” after losing seven consecutive elections for lower-level offices, was elected. He went from fewer than 10,000 votes in a mayoral race two years ago to 380,000 votes for congress.

During the campaign, Renato caused some friction within the family by saying that “Flávio is not Jair. He doesn’t draw crowds”. At the polls, however, Flávio ended up winning more votes than his father did in 2018 and 2022, although the result is seen by some as more of an anti-Lula vote than a strong preference for the senator.

The number of Bolsonaros in office could have been even higher had “son 03”, Eduardo Bolsonaro, 42, not abandoned his seat in congress and gone into self-imposed exile in the US, where for more than a year he has lobbied for what Lula and many others see as Donald Trump’s attempts to interfere in Brazil’s elections.

Although Michelle is the most recent member of the family to enter politics, it is she who is often considered to be the leading figure among the Bolsonaros. In a July poll, she was named the most powerful woman in Brazilian politics, well ahead of the current first lady, Janja Lula da Silva, in addition to a supreme court justice and many members of congress.

“She is a phenomenon,” said Camila Rocha, a researcher at the Brazilian Center for Analysis and Planning, who has interviewed voters and studied the Brazilian right for a decade. “Even Bolsonaro voters don’t like his sons very much, but many of them like Michelle, who is very charismatic.”

blocks.caption: Eduardo Bolsonaro with his father in São Paulo in June 2025. Photograph: ZUMA Press, Inc./Alamy

blocks.text: The daughter of a housewife and a retired bus driver from the metropolitan region around Brasília, Michelle was working as a parliamentary secretary for another politician when, at 25, she met Bolsonaro, then a 52-year-old congressman. She is his third wife.

When he took office as president in 2019, Michelle made history by becoming the first and only Brazilian first lady to deliver a speech at an inauguration. She did so in Brazilian Sign Language, which she had mastered while working as an interpreter at evangelical church services – her religiosity is seen as one of the main assets behind Bolsonaro’s close relationship with evangelical voters.

Despite playing by Bolsonaro’s party’s rules, Michelle was at the centre of one of the most contentious moments of Flávio Bolsonaro’s campaign, when she said that she had been “humiliated”, “disrespected” and “mistreated” by the senator. Reports of friction between her and her stepsons are frequent. Given her popularity, Flávio had to apologise publicly – although Michelle accepted it, the two did not campaign together.

Polls suggested Bolsonaro supporters would have preferred the former first lady as the presidential candidate, but the patriarch opted for his eldest son, and gave her the senate mission instead. “That was the mission my husband entrusted to me, and I will represent him, God willing,” she said in August.
Michelle and Bolsonaro’s sons were also widely seen as helping secure victories for other far-right candidates from Bolsonaro’s party, which will have by far the largest bloc in the next congress.
“Although the family has been in politics for a long time, many voters still see the Bolsonaros as representing ‘renewal’ and an anti-system vote,” said Rocha.
“So, to change everything, these voters want to throw a ‘bomb’ that blows up congress and Lula. And that bomb is the Bolsonaro family,” she added.

articles.title: Canada: Quebec separatists return to power, promise new independence referendum
articles.summary: Parti Quebecois has won the provincial election, but fallen short of a majority. Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon says he will seek another referendum on independence but not while US President Donald…

image.caption: The result returns Paul St-Pierre Plamondon’s party to power for the first time in more than a decadeImage: Mathieu Belanger/REUTERS

blocks.text: In the Quebec's provincial election on Monday the separatist Parti Quebecois (PQ) came in the lead after promising another referendum on independence from Canada but fell short of a outright majority.
The PQ, led by 49-year-old Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, was on track to win nearly 60 of the 127 seats in the National Assembly, just short of the 64 needed for a majority.
However, their return to power after more than a decade comes with a caveat as the minority government will need support from opposition parties to pass legislation and survive confidence votes.
"Quebecers elected the Parti Quebecois asking it to work with the other parties, and I heard that message," the PQ leader said.
St-Pierre Plamondon says dreams of independent Quebec
The PQ's return to power also brings to forefront the issue of identity of Quebec's French-speakers, who make up 80% of the population, and comes with a promise of an independence referendum.
St-Pierre Plamondon said he envisioned Quebec as a country on its own and that a referendum would allow Quebecers to decide their own future.
"I continue to dream and visualize that country," St-Pierre Plamondon said in his victory speech. "That dream will be realized one day."

The jubilant leader, however, made it clear that the referendum would not take place while US President Donald Trump remains in office. He said the decision would need "an informed and calm debate" and could not be allowed to be "hijacked by the theatrics of an unpredictable president."

blocks.caption: Coalition Avenir Quebec leader Christine Fréchette conceded defeat, saying voters had made their choice and that she took full responsibility for the "difficult result"Image: Mathieu Belanger/REUTERS

blocks.text: Severing ties with British monarchy?
The PQ's victory does not necessarily signal majority support for independence.
While in the last referendum for independence in 1995, just 50.58% to stay in Canada, recent polls show support for sovereignty at around 30%.
"If Quebec becomes independent it would make us politically, economically and militarily vulnerable," 19-year-old Alexia Gomez, 19 told news agency AFP.
The Liberals and Conservatives have also voiced their opposition to an independence referendum, further complicating the PQ's path.
On the other hand, in a move more likely to find resonance among Quebecers, St-Pierre Plamondon's party has also pledged to reduce Quebec's ties to the British monarchy.
Meanwhile, Monday's result comes just two weeks before Alberta voters decide whether to support beginning the process toward a referendum on separating from Canada.
Could Alberta separatists tear Canada apart?

articles.title: Badenoch calls for UK ‘Iron Dome’ missile defence system - UK politics live
articles.summary:
Conservatives plan ‘new integrated air and missile defence system to protect Britain from attack – in essence, a British “Iron Dome”’

Q: You are going to cut inheritance…

blocks.text: Badenoch does not accept claims £10bn not enough to fund missile defence
Jon Kay is interviewing Badenoch.
He puts it to her that the UK would need a very different missile defence system from Israel. Israel is under threat from short-range missiles, he says.
Badenoch says it is not just missiles that threaten the UK; drones are a threat too.
Q: Would £10bn be enough to pay for it?
Badenoch says it can be done. The £10bn would be spent over 10 years, she says. She says the UK needs to be protected.
Key events

items: 29s agoBadenoch claims 'we haven't called it Iron Dome' - despite Tories using phrase in their press release
12m agoBadenoch says Penny Mordaunt was 'fantastic MP' - but rules out special treatment for ex-MPs in candidate selection
18m agoBadenoch won't say whether speech tomorrow will include plan to cut inheritance tax
20m agoBadenoch does not accept claims £10bn not enough to fund missile defence
25m agoBadenoch pays tribute to Jeffrey Archer, saying he sent her supportive text hours before he died
29m agoLib Dems say Tories would only be able to get 'Patchwork Dome' for £10bn
33m agoWhat Tories are saying about how their proposed 'Britannia Shield' would work
40m agoPolitics Badenoch calls for UK ‘Iron Dome’ missile defence system

blocks.text: Badenoch claims 'we haven't called it Iron Dome' - despite Tories using phrase in their press release
Q: You say your Iron Dome will protect the whole of the UK, and bases abroad. But Sir Richard Barrons, the former general, has said that a proper air defence like this would cost up to £100bn.
Badenoch says Barrons is referring to an Israel-style Iron Dome.
She says she is referring to something different. She says the UK should be able to defend itself from, for example, someone on a boat firing a drone at the system.
Q: But it is nothing like Israel’s Iron Dome. It is a gimmick, isn’t it?
Badenoch replied:
double quotation markIt’s not going to be exactly like the Irone Dome. We haven’t called it an Iron Dome.
But, in fact, they did. This is what they sent out to journalists yesterday.

blocks.caption: Press release Photograph: Conservative party

blocks.text: Badenoch is on Times Radio now. She is being interviewed by Kate McCann.
Asked when she would raise defence spending to 3.5% of GDP, Badenoch says she has a plan to get to 3%. But she is not in government.
Q: But you say there might be an election soon?
Badenoch says the 3.5% is a Nato target.
She says she is not in government, and she implies it is unreasonable for McCann to expect her to set out a path to 3.5% when she is not in government.
Badenoch says Penny Mordaunt was 'fantastic MP' - but rules out special treatment for ex-MPs in candidate selection
Q: Would you like to see Penny Mordaunt selected as a Tory candidate?

(At the weekend Mordaunt, the former cabinet minister who lost her seat at the election, revealed she has been approved for the candidates list, which means she can apply to be a candidate in a Tory seat.)
Badenoch says it is not up to her to decide; local parties choose their candidates, she says.
She says she wants “serious people” committed to public service as MPs.
Q: Do you want to see her selected?
Badenoch says Mordaunt was a “fantastic MP”. She says she was sorry she lost her seat, and is glad she wants to stand again.
But former MPs won’t get special treatment when candidates are being selected, she says. She says she wants candidate selection to be a “meritocracy”.
Badenoch won't say whether speech tomorrow will include plan to cut inheritance tax
Q: You are going to cut inheritance tax, aren’t you?
Badenoch says everyone knows she would like to do that. She has said that before.
But she won’t announce that unless she has found the money to pay for it.
Q: Will you have found the money by the time you give your speech tomorrow?
Badenoch tells Kay he will have to wait.
Badenoch pays tribute to Jeffrey Archer, saying he sent her supportive text hours before he died
Kemi Badenoch is on BBC Breakfast.
They start by asking about the death of Jeffrey Archer, and Badenoch says she got a message from him only yesterday morning. He said: “Great outfit, great speech, no need to reply.”
Badenoch says Archer was “a great communicator” and a “great storyteller”, and someone who believed in Conservatism.
Here is our story about his death.
Lib Dems say Tories would only be able to get 'Patchwork Dome' for £10bn

The Liberal Democrats have dismissed the Tory plan for a “Britannia Shield” as “Truss-style fantasy economics”. They say the Conservatives would only get a “Patchwork Dome” with the £10bn they plan to spend on the project.
James MacCleary, the Lib Dem defence spokesperson, said:

double quotation markOnce again the Conservatives are indulging in Truss-style fantasy economics. £10bn would not even touch the sides for a complete UK-wide ‘Iron Dome’. They either need to review their dodgy sums or come clean about which parts of the country their Patchwork Dome wouldn’t cover. Let’s not forget this is the party that hollowed out our armed forces for a decade, and whose disgraceful plan to fill the defence-spending black hole is based on targeted cuts to the poorest and most vulnerable children. You do not make Britain safer by pushing families into poverty.
What Tories are saying about how their proposed 'Britannia Shield' would work
This is what the Conservatives are saying about why the UK needs a “Britannia Shield” (their name for what they describe as a version of the “Iron Dome”), and who it would work.

double quotation markThe announcement comes as the threat of missile and drone attack against Britain and our allies continues to grow. Russia bombards Ukraine daily with ever more advanced drones and missiles, and they were behind a drone attack on Leipzig airport in August. Drones launched by Iranian proxies have hit our RAF base in Cyprus, and when Iran fired missiles at the Chagos islands earlier this year, it was the US who stepped in to launch interceptors. Nato allies, especially in the Baltic States, are suffering ever greater numbers of drone incursions and western intelligence agencies have warned that Russia could attack a Nato country by 2030. We live in an increasingly dangerous and unpredictable world, where threats to the UK and our allies are growing in scale and complexity, yet Britain remains dangerously exposed. A report in November 2025 by the defence select committee warned that, compared to European allies investing heavily in integrated air and missile defence, the UK has “next to nothing”. The Conservatives will close this dangerous capability gap by committing up to £10 billion over ten years. We will deliver a minimal deployable capability within our first term in office, with the remaining investment focused on expanding and strengthening the system over time. Britannia Shield will have three key components: SENSE: New advanced radar systems, to detect incoming missiles and drones. DECIDE: Upgraded command and control systems to integrate information from across Britain’s defences and rapidly identify the most effective response. EFFECT: New interceptor missiles, counter-drone capabilities, and significantly larger missile stockpiles to defeat incoming threats.
Politics Badenoch calls for UK ‘Iron Dome’ missile defence system

Good morning. Kemi Badenoch is doing a round of interviews this morning at the Conservative conference, and she will be talking about her plans for the UK to have its own version of Israel’s “Iron Dome” missile defence system. That phrase is not just journalists’ hype; it has come from the first line of the party’s press release, which says the party has plans for a “new integrated air and missile defence system to protect Britain from attack – in essence, a British ‘Iron Dome’.”
Here is our story by Jessica Elgot and Dan Sabbagh.
And this is what Badenoch is saying about it.

double quotation markThe first duty of government is to defend the country and keep people safe. Labour are failing that basic test. The world will not wait for Britain to get ready. War has returned to Europe. Missiles and drones are transforming warfare in the Middle East. Cheap weapons can now threaten cities, military bases and critical infrastructure in ways that would have sounded like science fiction a generation ago. If a missile or drone is launched at Britain, we do not get a second chance to wish we had prepared.

The Tories say their plan would cost £1bn a year over 10 years, and that the money would come from the plan they announced last month to raise defence spending by £10bn a year. Almost half the money for this would come from cuts to housing benefit.
Here is the agenda for the day.
7.30am: Kemi Badenoch begins a round of media interviews, starting with BBC Breakfast.

9.45am: The morning session of the Conservative party conference opens, with speeches from Katie Lam, the shadow housing secretary, then Laura Trott, the shadow education secretary (at 10.30am) and Rebecca Paul, the shadow culture secretary (at noon).

2pm: The afternoon session starts, with speeches from Alex Burghart, the deputy leader, Tom Tugendhat, the shadow foreign secretary, James Cartlidge, the shadow defence secretary, and Helen Whately, the shadow work and pensions secretary.

I’m afraid we are no longer able to have comments open below the line every day on this blog. If you want to contact me, please email politics.live@theguardian.com. You can use this email to flag up corrections, comments for publication, questions or complaints.

articles.title: Nigeria mourns as 32 killed in military plane crash
articles.summary: President Bola Tinubu describes the crash as a "painful moment" for the military and the entire nation.

blocks.text: Nigeria's President Bola Tinubu has declared three days of national mourning after a military aircraft crashed in southern Ondo State, killing 32 people.
Authorities say the plane was on a routine mission from Benin City to Lagos when it came down near a naval base on Monday morning.
A resident told the BBC that the plane had crashed near a swamp and that clothes and shoes had been found at the site. Smoke could be seen rising from the area.
Tinubu offered his deepest condolences for the 25 passengers and seven crew members on board and has ordered a full investigation.
The president also ordered national flags to be flown at half-mast across the country as a mark of respect for those who died.
"This is a painful moment for our Armed Forces and for the entire nation," Tinubu said.
"Our Air Force personnel put their lives on the line every day to secure Nigeria. Their sacrifice will never be forgotten," he added.
Aviation Minister Festus Keyamo earlier said he had been informed "of the disappearance of a military aircraft with tail number NGR 931, enroute Lagos from Benin at 0913 hours earlier today".
He said "efforts to raise the aircraft on radio proved abortive" before subsequent confirmation that it had crashed near a naval base in Igbokoda, Ondo state.
He said search and rescue efforts were ongoing.
The crashed plane, described as an ATR-42 aircraft, carries between 30 and 50 passengers, according to its manufacturers.
Tinubu has ordered the Air Force to immediately begin a thorough investigation into the cause of the crash to help prevent similar incidents in the future.
The identities of those who died have not yet been released. Authorities say the names of the officers will be published after their families have been informed.
The Nigerian Air Force plays a key role in the country's military operations, including efforts to tackle armed groups and insecurity in several parts of the country.
The accident is one ​of the deadliest air disasters ​in ⁠Nigeria in recent years.
In May 2021, Nigeria's army chief, Lt-Gen Ibrahim Attahiru, was killed in a plane crash alongside 10 other officers in the north-western state of Kaduna amid bad weather.
In February of the same year, seven people died after a military plane crashed short of a runway in the capital Abuja.

articles.title: From competing for food to a gold medal: the stories behind India’s Asian Games winners
articles.summary:
The country’s 85-medal haul included athletes who trained with limited money and borrowed equipment. Plus, the Mumbai performer turning everyday absurdities into comedy

In a country where…

blocks.text: In a country where cricket eclipses every other sport, the recently concluded Asian Games offered a much-needed reminder of India’s breadth of sporting talent. In this edition of the games, in Japan, India won 85 medals: 21 golds, 27 silver and 37 bronze medals. I admit I did not know many of the players competing, or even some of the sports they play before putting this piece together. Learning about the stories, I wonder why not.
There were individual breakthroughs, records broken and history made. There were also hard-fought team victories, including the Indian women’s hockey team gold medal after a 44-year wait.

Sports broadcaster Siddharth Pandey cited an old saying in the world of sport: “You cannot be what you cannot see.” For Pandey, one of the most heartening sights was families and communities rallying around the four female players from the north-eastern states. (The region has endured decades of conflict and is often overlooked in the national conversation.) “We simply cannot underestimate the impact these games and medals have on future generations taking up non-cricketing sport and wanting to excel in it,” he told me.

Recognition is also important. Vidya Pillai, the first Indian woman to win a snooker world championship has spoken about her sport not getting the attention or respect it deserves. She felt unacknowledged following her 2023 feat, despite the fact that it came after six unsuccessful world finals and she beat two former world champions along the way.
Behind India’s medal glory are dozens of athletes and families who have struggled financially, trained with limited facilities, and often without much institutional support.

blocks.caption: Indian athletes at the closing ceremony of the 2026 Asian Games, in Japan. Photograph: Chalinee Thirasupa/Reuters

blocks.text: So this week, I am sharing a sample of the many extraordinary stories from different parts of the country. These are only a fraction of the champions to emerge from the games, yet they provide a glimpse of the possibilities that can open up when a country sees and celebrates sporting talent across the spectrum.

Neeru Dhanda (gold in trap shooting): Dhanda’s family in Haryana’s Jind relies on the government’s food subsidy programme and she began her sporting journey using a borrowed shotgun with tin cans as targets. Right before the games began, the 26-year-old spent a few days in a hospital recovering from an illness instead of training. But last week, as rain lashed the shooting range in Urenocho, she became the first Indian woman to win an individual gold in trap shooting at Asian games. She won a second gold in mixed team trap event as well as a silver in the women’s team trap event.

Vithya Ramraj (gold in 4x400m): Ramraj was one of the breakout stars of the event with a three-medal haul. NDTV reported that her father had to borrow money to support Ramraj and her twin sister’s athletic careers. Alongside the team gold in 4x400m, she won a silver in the mixed 4x400m relay. She also broke Indian legend PT Usha’s long-held national record in 400m hurdles which won her a bronze medal.

Sahil Jadhav (gold in compound mixed archery team and men’s compound team): Not long ago, Jadhav contemplated quitting archery, frustrated by not making the progress he had hoped for. He had been forced to compete with borrowed arrows for selection trials, the New Indian Express reported, adding that his mother sold her jewellery to buy him professional compound bows. Now, the 25-year-old has two gold medals and an automatic entry to the 2028 LA Olympics.

Lalremsiami Hmarzote (member of the gold-winning women’s hockey team): The women’s hockey team forward once had to travel about 100 miles from her home to reach the only hockey academy in Mizoram. When she was growing up, her parents had no idea about what hockey and she played barefoot on dirt pitches. This month, playing her 200th international appearance, the 26-year-old struck gold. She scored the lone goal of the final against China, which Hockey India described as a “stunning reverse-stick strike”.

Ancy Sojan (silver in long jump): With colourful beads glistening in her hair, Sojan flung herself 6.53 metres in long jump, to win the silver medal. Earlier this year, the 25-year-old broke the national record set in 2004. Her journey, from a village in Kerala’s Thrissur district to the international stage, has not been straightforward. Last year, she was diagnosed with polycystic ovarian syndrome, forcing her to drastically change her diet and manage the medication-related weight gain she had before the tournament.

Aslam Inamdar (a member of the gold-winning men’s kabaddi team): Inamdar came to kabaddi, a south Asian contact sport combining elements of tag and wrestling, from humble beginnings – he was partly drawn to it because it was affordable and didn’t require expensive equipment. Coming from a village in Maharashtra’s Ahilyanagar, he worked odd jobs – from cleaning washrooms to working in the fields – so he could spend evenings training. “It still feels like a dream to me,” Inamdar told the Indian Express. “I often think about how someone who didn’t even have food at home now holds two international medals.” The 26-year-old was instrumental in helping India win their gold-medal match against Iran.
I would love to hear from you: which sportsperson from the Asian Games did you find most inspiring and why?
What else we’re reading about

blocks.caption: A tribute to pilot Smit Machchhar, whose swift actions helped save the lives of 174 passengers on a flydubai flight to Israel. Photograph: AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Flydubai incident | Indian pilot Smit Machchar is being hailed as a hero for helping to save 174 passengers on the flydubai flight to Israel last week, after his co-pilot made an apparent effort to crash the plane. After being stabbed, Machchar opened the cockpit door, allowing passengers and crew to enter and overpower the attacker. He is recovering in a hospital in Saudi Arabia, where the plane eventually landed.

Datacentres | Protests against water-guzzling datacentres erupting from the US to Australia are gathering momentum in India. South Asia correspondent Hannah Ellis-Petersen travelled to the small village of Tarluvada, in Andhra Pradesh, where the state government has been accused of fast-tracking plans for a $15bn AI datacentre for Google, allegedly to avoid stringent environmental scrutiny.

Art and design | Designer Vikram Goyal, celebrated for his signature repoussé brass work, brings his installation Wings and Tales to a Georgian townhouse in London’s Mayfair from 12 to 16 October. The exhibition includes furniture designs inspired by landscapes from the Indian epic Ramayana.
Guest shelf
A recommendation from someone with great taste
after newsletter promotion

blocks.caption: A detail of Al-Qawi Nanavati’s work.

blocks.text: Shireen Gandhy, director of Mumbai’s pioneering Chemould Prescott Road Gallery, founded in 1963, recommends the work of artist Al-Qawi Nanavati. “[She] is a young artist from Bombay whose practice is rooted in printmaking and making her own paper. Her mother’s passing left her with a void,” says Gandhy. Nanavati created Letters to My Mother, an epistolary artwork crafted in, as Gandhy puts it, “a deeply personal language that is not known to anybody but her. Using fabrics and saris that belonged to her mother, she creates this tactile imagery for these letters. I find it very moving and like alchemy.”
Count it
A number worth knowing

blocks.caption: Students at a cram school in Kota, where every year hundreds of thousands of students take the Indian Institutes of Technology exam. Photograph: Saurabh Das/AP

blocks.text: This is the number of students from disadvantaged communities who dropped out of some of India’s most prestigious institutions: central universities, Indian Institutes of Technology and Indian Institutes of Management between 2018 and 2023, according to Anubhuti Vishnoi of the Economic Times. The figure comes from an interim report by a committee set up by the supreme court last year to examine mental health and suicide prevention in higher education.
Vibe check

blocks.caption: Nitesh Shetty plays know-it-all for laughs. Photograph: Instagram/@ nitesh_shetty99

blocks.text: Nitesh Shetty’s sketches find absurdity in everyday life, turning familiar characters and social interactions into unexpected punchlines. This is what makes his work powerful: you’re laughing one moment and moved the next. There is a reel for every character imaginable: the person perpetually trapped in the limbo of land disputes, the man who is strangely knowledgeable about funerals, or the friend who has a unique dressing sense.

The 35-year-old from Mumbai didn’t plan on a career in comedy. “When you don’t know what to do, you try anything,” he told me. Now, Shetty rejects more conventional formats such as television in favour of challenging himself creatively. His advice for those who look up to him? “It’s a great time to build something. The [online] audience is ready-made for you. Be original and don’t follow trends.”
Get in touch

Do you have any thoughts or responses to this week’s newsletter? Is there anything you’d like us to cover in the future? Share your feedback by replying to this, or emailing us at thisisindia@theguardian.com and we may include your response in a future issue.

image.caption: Tobias Rausch has been elected as speaker in Saxony-Anhalt's parliamentImage: Jan Woitas/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: October 6, 2026
Far-right AfD candidate elected state parliamentary speaker

blocks.caption: Tobias Rausch has been in the Saxony-Anhalt parliament since 2016Image: dts-Agentur/picture alliance

blocks.text: Tobias Rausch, the far-right Alternative for Germany's (AFD's) nomination for speaker in Saxony-Anhalt's state parliament, has been elected with the help of the populist BSW party.
Rausch gained 48 votes from 82 eligible votes. There were five abstentions.

The AfD holds 39 seats in the parliament and the BSW five, giving Rausch the majority he needed to win the post, as the other parties combined — all of which reject working with the AfD — also hold 39 seats.
The result means that member of parties besides the AfD and BSW voted for him.

Rausch, 35, thus becomes the first member of the AfD — a party classified by domestic intelligence in Saxony-Anhalt as a "confirmed right-wing extremist" organization — to become speaker in a state parliament in Germany.
The new speaker is a real-estate entrepreneur by profession and has been a member of parliament for the AfD in Saxony-Anhalt since 2016.
The parliamentary session was accompanied by several anti-AfD protests in front of the parliament building.

The company's chief strategy officer Jason Kwon faced a parliamentary hearing into AI on Tuesday in Sydney, saying the breach "should not have happened" and it "should have handled our response better". It took weeks before Australia was notified via an email to a generic inbox.
"We are sorry and we know we have work to do to rebuild trust with the Australian people," Kwon said.
Anthropic also appeared and said it had not found any cases of Australian breaches during a recent investigation.

An OpenAI agent went "rogue" and "infiltrated" a private statistics portal containing "non-sensitive" data from Australia's universal healthcare scheme Medicare in June in what cyber-security experts said was the first hack of its kind.
Asked why OpenAI had not directly contacted government ministers immediately after it found out about the breaches, Kwon acknowledged it was a mistake.
"In retrospect, we should have done what you're suggesting," Kwon said, in response to a question by the committee on why it had not dialled the mobile numbers of government ministers.
"The reason why it happened the way that it did is I think people were thinking about this as a technical situation and they wanted to contact the technical counterparties but it's not good enough."
Kwon said the company has changed how it handles such incidents.
"Even if we don't fully understand the situation, we are just going to notify and start working through the situation collaboratively with the impacted party."

OpenAI has also added "more precautions" to its training environments since the incidents, Kwon told the 12-member committee which is made up of Labor, Liberal and independent MPs and senators who are looking at AI and its impact on Australia.
The company was also establishing a local taskforce in Australia to investigate "how to better manage the risks associated with increasingly capable AI".
Kwon told the committee that training models were now monitored in real time during tests, and an alarm was triggered if they interact with the internet in a way they were not meant to.
This meant that it had been able to alert the New South Wales government to another hack last week within 48 hours.
The company would also support a framework on mandatory disclosure of incidents, Kwon said, as it would set out "clear expectations".
"We were trying to come up with a standard to apply to our voluntary actions… based on our learned experience here, we should have been probably talking to more people about how to do that well."

Anthropic's head of safeguards Dave Orr said in the wake of OpenAI agents hacking tech platform Hugging Face in July, it had reviewed "hundreds of millions of transcripts" to detect any potential breaches of Australian government websites similar to OpenAI.
"We haven't found anything like this and we have looked," he told the committee.
The public hearings, which will continue until Friday, also heard evidence from arts and media organisations about copyright and their concerns on how AI models use their materials.

An opt-out model - where the onus would be on the artist to ask AI not to use their material for training purposes - was flawed and could means artists do not get paid for their content, the committee heard.
"In other words, Australia's artists will be the roadkill in the rush to this AI deal," said Annabelle Herd, chief executive of the Australian Recording Industry Association.
